claim.pdf_says: 9.3.7   Method prototypes ... 9.3.8   Conformance and interfaces / 9.3.8.1   General -- third-level subsections of 9.3 Objects, printed identically to 9.3.6 Method invocation which immediately precedes them.
claim.markdown_says: ## 9.3.7 Method prototypes ... ## 9.3.8 Conformance and interfaces ... ### 9.3.8.1 General -- level 2, i.e. the SAME level as their parent '## 9.3 Objects' and one level above their own sibling '### 9.3.6 Method invocation'.
claim.why_it_matters: In the generated outline/TOC, 9.3.7 and 9.3.8 detach from 9.3 Objects and appear as peers of it, while 9.3.8.1 (level 3) then appears as a peer of 9.3.6. The section hierarchy the markdown advertises contradicts the numbering, so heading-level-driven navigation and any doc tooling that derives structure from '#' depth mis-nests this whole run of object-orientation rules.

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED on three independent grounds.

(1) NOTHING IS MISSING. The claim is filed as kind=missing-heading, but all three headings are present in specs/ISO_COBOL.md with their clause numbers and titles transcribed verbatim and correctly: line 12073 '## 9.3.7 Method prototypes', line 12078 '## 9.3.8 Conformance and interfaces', line 12081 '### 9.3.8.1 General'. Each also carries a correct hierarchical anchor (<a id="section-9-3-7">, section-9-3-8, section-9-3-8-1). Body text on the page matches the PDF. No PDF text is absent, altered, or misquoted; the claim quotes both sources accurately.

(2) THE PDF CARRIES NO LEVEL INFORMATION FOR THE MARKDOWN TO LOSE. I rendered page 276 at 300 dpi and zoomed the heading block (E:/Temp/specrecon/v276/headings.png). '9.3.7   Method prototypes', '9.3.8   Conformance and interfaces' and '9.3.8.1   General' are printed in IDENTICAL typography -- same bold face, same point size, same left margin, same number/title tab. I also rendered page 272 (E:/Temp/specrecon/v272/spec_p272.png), where '9.3.6   Method invocation' is printed in that same identical style. So ISO does not typographically distinguish clause level 3 from clause level 4 anywhere in this run. The claim's premise -- that the PDF marks 9.3.7/9.3.8 as one level and 9.3.8.1 as another, and the markdown flattened that distinction -- is false: the PDF marks them all the same. The ONLY hierarchy signal the PDF emits is the dotted clause number itself, and the markdown reproduces every clause number exactly. Zero information is lost in transcription.

(3) THE '#' DEPTHS ARE A DOCUMENT-WIDE TRANSCRIPTION ARTIFACT, NOT A PAGE-276 DISCREPANCY. Of 2098 numbered headings in specs/ISO_COBOL.md, the '#' depth is essentially uncorrelated with the number depth: 3-component headings appear as h2 276 times, h3 508 times, h4 17 times; 4-component headings appear as h2 162 times, h3 620 times, h4 24 times; 5-component as h2 118 / h3 128 / h4 41. Even the immediate neighbourhood is arbitrary -- '### 9.1 Files' is h3 while '## 9.2 Screens' and '## 9.3 Objects' are h2; 9.1.3-9.1.7, 9.1.7.3, 9.1.7.4, 9.1.8, 9.1.8.1, 9.2.5-9.2.7, 9.3.5.2, 9.3.5.3, 9.3.8.2, 9.3.13, 9.3.14 are all h2. Any tool deriving structure from '#' depth is already wrong on ~2000 headings; page 276 is in no way a distinguishing instance, and 'fixing' these three lines would not make the outline correct.

This falls squarely under the reject criterion 'the difference is only ... formatting' and 'the difference does not change meaning'. A reader or tool consuming '9.3.7' knows unambiguously that it is a subsection of 9.3 regardless of the '#' count. If markdown heading depths are wanted to track clause numbering, that is a single global normalization pass over the whole file (mechanically derivable from the number), not a per-page reconciliation finding against the PDF.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a PDF-vs-markdown content discrepancy. All three headings (9.3.7, 9.3.8, 9.3.8.1) are present on page 276 with numbers and titles transcribed exactly; nothing is missing or misquoted. The PDF prints 9.3.6, 9.3.7, 9.3.8 and 9.3.8.1 in identical bold type at identical size and margin, so it encodes hierarchy solely through the clause number -- which the markdown preserves perfectly. The observation that the '#' depth does not track the clause numbering is true but is a global property of the transcription (2039 of 2098 numbered headings deviate from any consistent number-to-depth rule; '### 9.1 Files' vs '## 9.2 Screens' vs '## 9.3 Objects' in the same clause), so it belongs in a one-time whole-file heading-depth normalization task, not in the per-page PDF reconciliation ledger.
